Kevin Lamarque | Reuters South Korea's $200 billion investment into the U.S., which President Donald Trump said would transform America "for generations," is not a done deal in totality. The South Korean investment plan includes nuclear power plants, a natural gas power facility in Texas and potentially the long-planned Alaska LNG project. Trump in a Truth Social post late Wednesday stateside said the countries had agreed to work on the Alaska LNG project, pegging its value at $50 billion, drawing a response from South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung, who emphasized that involvement in some of the projects remains subject to commercial considerations. Lee in an X post on Thursday local time said that participation in the Alaska LNG project was dependent on its financial viability and legal compliance. He added that investments in nuclear power plants would also require assessment of commercial viability on a plant-by-plant basis. Trump had hailed South Korean investments in his post late Wednesday stateside, saying that the countries had agreed to work on the Alaska LNG project, pegging its value at $50 billion. The joint statement earlier on Wednesday, however, had mentioned that work on the project was contingent on "commercial reasonableness," without highlighting details on allocations toward the project. The Alaska LNG project seeks to transport natural gas roughly 1,300 kilometers from fields on Alaska's North Slope to the southern part of the state, where it would be liquefied for export to markets including Asia, reported Yonhap. The project has faced longstanding questions over its economics given the large upfront investment required. Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan had described it as "high-risk" last year and said participation would be difficult unless it could generate sufficient cash flow. Overall, the investment package includes $22.3 billion for a 6,472-megawatt natural gas power facility in Encinal, Texas, that will supply electricity to co-located data centers. The project will be led by developer Related Companies and U.S. power company NextEra Energy, with the first phase expected to begin commercial operations in 2029 and the full facility coming online in stages by 2032. Trump said the investments would turn South Korea's commitments into "huge construction projects" and create "tens of thousands of American jobs." "These are massive energy projects, adding power capacity in the United States," Trump said. "This is new construction, new manufacturing, and great jobs for American workers." The two countries said they would seek to expand Korean companies' participation in the Texas project across equipment supply, engineering and construction, as well as long-term operations and maintenance. The U.S. also intends to give Korean companies opportunities to supply equipment, including turbines, to similar projects in the country. Another $120 billion has been allocated to plans for eight large-scale nuclear reactors in the U.S. Of that amount, $100 billion is earmarked for construction costs and $20 billion for contingency reserves. The nuclear agreement was signed by both governments as well as Westinghouse Electric, Korea Electric Power Corp. and Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power. The plan also calls for pursuing a potential significant minority investment in Westinghouse by Korean companies, with the terms subject to commercial negotiations. Trump’s AI lunch included every major tech company. Except Apple
headlines.summary: Apple's absence from Trump's AI lunch raised eyebrows, but the company is known to look out for its own interests.
headlines.article_text: Trump’s AI lunch included everyone but Apple Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points President Donald Trump's gathering of the world's most powerful tech companies didn't include one notable company: Apple. Former CEO Tim Cook now acts as Apple's public face with government officials around the world, and he maintains a good relationship with Trump. While every other major U.S. tech company was represented, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner called Apple's absence a "nothing burger." In this article AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, stands with U.S. President Donald Trump, Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta Platforms, Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson (R-LA) and others holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence outside the West Wing of the White House on Sept. 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. Kevin Dietsch | Getty Images When President Donald Trump gathered execs from the world's most powerful tech companies in the White House on Tuesday to discuss the future of artificial intelligence, one company was conspicuously absent: Apple . Neither Chairman Tim Cook nor his successor as CEO, John Ternus, were present, while leaders from every other tech megacap – and many other companies – lunched with Trump. Apple didn't respond to CNBC's questions about the meeting, nor did the White House. Social media buzzed with conjecture that Apple wasn't invited because the company is behind on AI. Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, a powerhouse investor in Silicon Valley and a Trump ally in the second term, called Apple's absence a " nothing burger " int an interview with CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday. "I can assure you, they're very much read in on all of this, and I suspect they agree with all of it," Gerstner said. Cook, as Apple's public face with government officials around the world, was at the White House less than a week ago, when he attended Trump's state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Gerstner pointed out. U.S. President Donald Trump walks past Apple CEO Tim Cook at the U.S. Ambassador's Residence in Tokyo, Japan, October 28, 2025. Evelyn Hockstein | Reuters Cook stepped down as Apple CEO in September, handing the baton to hardware specialist Ternus. As part of the transition, Apple noted that Cook would still handle "engaging with policymakers around the world" as the company's executive chairman. His new role was underscored last week at the state dinner with Xi. Over the years, Cook has put in the time to maintain a good relationship with Trump. He's made over 10 public appearances at events in the president's second term, including Trump's inauguration, in the oval office, at Davos, and at state dinners on multiple continents. He attended the "Melania" screening at the White House. Throughout his dealings with Trump over the past two years, Cook has stayed on message, focused on Apple's manufacturing interests and trade issues, at a time where its products could be subject to tariffs . The company has given the Trump administration wins on issues like American investment and jobs while trying to ward off Trump's longstanding desire for the company to make iPhones in the U.S. More recently, Apple has reportedly sought to use Chinese-made memory chips as prices skyrocket around the world, but doing so requires a license. Commerce Secretary Lutnick said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal that "the Trump administration is not in favor of that." A different approach Gerstner, in his CNBC interview, said that the participants at the lunch were the companies that were "really pushing the frontier on model development." That's not Apple. The iPhone makers' in-house models are smaller and more efficient than the so-called "frontier" models developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, which were both represented. Apple Foundation Models are mostly designed to run on Apple's own silicon inside iPhones and Mac computers. They run parts of Siri, while OpenAI and Anthropic's models use massive Nvidia -based clusters of chips. Apple is a consumer company, whereas most of the frontier lab AI competition happens in the enterprise. Apple partners with Google to develop its models. Its capital expenditures are tiny compared to the sums Google, Microsoft , Meta , and Amazon are investing. While some investors fret that Apple is falling behind in AI, the market has increasingly seen it as a hedge to other capex-heavy tech names. And the company just launched a new AI-powered Siri earlier to mostly positive reviews. watch now VIDEO 4:21 04:21 How the AI industry will self-regulate AI safety News Videos Apple's stock is up 22.5% so far in 2026, outpacing the Nasdaq and almost all of its megacap peers other than Nvidia, which is up about the same amount. Though Apple is very much touting the power of AI and its role in the technology's future, company executives have been mostly absent from the public debate around AI safety or alignment, which were primary topics at Trump's luncheon. Nobody at Apple has penned the long manifestos like the ones coming from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft and others. As part of Tuesday's meeting with Trump, the White House and the leading AI companies signed an accord, committing the industry players to various safety measures. After the meeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI COO Greg Brockman, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei all signed the document. Cook has said several times over the years that Apple is more likely to weigh in publicly on policy that "intersects with our company in some way." Apple's not dealing with alignment issues on the frontier. "If it doesn't intersect — if it's something where we would just be another voice out there and not have a unique perspective to bring — then we don't say anything," Cook said in a 2021 DealBook interview.
